raw_case_text: A 9-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with a 2-month history of 10-15 bouts of mucoid bloody diarrhoea per day and crampy lower abdominal pain that was relieved after defaecation. She lost weight, was fatigued and had oral aphthous lesions. Except for consanguinity, her family history was unremarkable. She was pale and growth retarded [height 120 cm (<3s%), body weight 16.2 kg (<3s%) and height standard deviation score 1.92]. Physical examination revealed aphthous lesions on the gingiva, an anal fissure, hyperaemic perianal skin tags, and increased bowel sounds. Laboratory data (with their normal range in parentheses) were: haemoglobin level (Hb) 8.2 g/dl (10.9-13.3 g/dl), mean corpuscular volume 62.9 fl (77-95 fl), platelet count 646,000/mm3 (183,000-369,000/mm3), white blood cell count 25,400/mm3 (4,700-10,300/mm3), C-reactive protein level (CRP) 9.2 mg/dl (<0.1 mg/dl), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 48 mm/h (0-20 mm/h), serum albumin level 2.8 g/dl (3.7-5.6 g/dl) and protein level 4.8 g/dl (5.9-8 g/dl). Leucocytes and erythrocytes were found in the stool, but no enteric pathogens were seen. The endoscopic and histopathological findings of the colon and terminal ileum were compatible with CD. She was put on prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day). Her complaints resolved, and laboratory tests improved during the second week. After 4 weeks of steroid treatment, mesalamine was added for the first time, and the steroid was tapered by 5 mg/week. The day after stopping prednisolone, while taking only mesalamine, she had a fever (38.5 C), abdominal pain, nausea and bloody mucoid diarrhoea (8-9 times per day). Her physical examination was normal except for the anal fissure. Laboratory tests showed a platelet count of 546,000/mm3, white blood cell count of 12,500/mm3, ESR of 45 mm/h and a CRP level of 8.6 mg/dl; gross blood and mucus were seen in the stool, but bacterial pathogens and parasites were negative. Urine, throat and blood cultures, viral markers, and Toxoplasma, Brucella and Salmonella were negative, ruling out acute infection. This clinical picture was compatible with an acute exacerbation of the disease. She was given her first dosage of infliximab (5 mg/kg) because of the serious side effects caused by the steroid treatment. Broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment was begun. However, her fever persisted and increased to 39.9 C with shivering and did not differ between day and night; there were frequent bowel movements (20-22/day) with blood and mucus and increased inflammatory serological markers. At that point, mesalamine was thought to be the cause of the fever, mimicking CD, and the drug was discontinued. Her temperature normalised, and the frequency of bowel movement decreased to 3-4/day within 36 h. Three days after stopping the mesalamine treatment, she had no more complaints. The inflammatory markers decreased significantly within 1 week. She was put on azathioprine, and no exacerbation was observed during the 2-year follow-up period.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 2-month history of 10-15 bouts of mucoid bloody diarrhea daily, crampy lower abdominal pain relieved by defecation, weight loss, fatigue, and oral aphthous ulcers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 9-year-old girl presented with 2 months of severe mucoid bloody diarrhea (10-15 stools/day), crampy lower abdominal pain, fatigue, weight loss, and oral aphthae. After colonoscopy confirmed Crohn's disease, she responded to 4 weeks of oral prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day), after which mesalamine was introduced and prednisolone tapered off; the day after stopping prednisolone (while on mesalamine monotherapy), she developed acute high fever (38.5 C rising to 39.9 C with rigors), nausea, abdominal pain, and severe bloody mucoid diarrhea (8-9 rising to 20-22 stools/day) refractory to infliximab (5 mg/kg) and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to consanguineous parents; no other significant family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for frequent bloody mucoid diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, weight loss, growth retardation, fatigue, oral aphthae, and subsequent mesalamine-induced high fever (39.9 C), rigors, and nausea.

objective.physical_examination: Pale and severely growth-retarded: height 120 cm (<3rd percentile, height SDS -1.92), weight 16.2 kg (<3rd percentile). Gingival aphthous ulcers, hyperemic perianal skin tags, anal fissure, and hyperactive bowel sounds. During the post-steroid mesalamine flare, temperature spiked to 38.5-39.9 C with rigors.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hb 8.2 g/dL (normal: 10.9-13.3), MCV 62.9 fL (77-95), platelets 646,000/mm3 (183,000-369,000), WBC 25,400/mm3 (4,700-10,300), CRP 9.2 mg/dL (<0.1), ESR 48 mm/h (0-20), serum albumin 2.8 g/dL (3.7-5.6), total protein 4.8 g/dL (5.9-8.0). Stool microscopy showed abundant leukocytes and erythrocytes with negative enteric bacterial and parasitic pathogens. Flare labs on mesalamine: platelets 546,000/mm3, WBC 12,500/mm3, ESR 45 mm/h, CRP 8.6 mg/dL; urine, throat, and blood cultures, viral markers, and Toxoplasma, Brucella, and Salmonella serologies were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Colonoscopy, ileoscopy, and mucosal biopsy histopathology of the colon and terminal ileum confirmed Crohn's disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Endoscopic histopathology confirmed ileocolonic Crohn's disease, and negative infectious workup (including Brucella, Salmonella, and Toxoplasma) alongside rapid clinical resolution within 36-72 hours of drug withdrawal confirmed mesalamine-induced acute intolerance syndrome (fever and exacerbation of bloody diarrhea mimicking a severe Crohn's flare). Following mesalamine discontinuation, she was maintained on oral azathioprine and remained in complete clinical remission over 2 years of follow-up.
